Employment Scams

Recruitment Agency Scams UK: Spot a Fake Job Offer

Fraudsters can impersonate recruitment agencies or misuse real company details—verify the agency, vacancy and contact route independently.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-05-08 · Updated 2026-08-06 · 9 min read

Quick answer: Agencies generally cannot charge individual applicants for finding work, although defined exceptions and separately chargeable services exist. A prohibited charge is a warning, not proof the agency is fictitious. Verify the agency independently before paying or sending documents, and report suspected fraud to Report Fraud or Police Scotland on 101.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What a recruitment-agency scam looks like

A recruitment-agency scam uses a fake or impersonated agency to take your money, identity documents, bank details, or access to your account. A recruiter contacts you about a strong role, then asks for an upfront fee, early ID, bank details, or help moving money. An example of the style is: We would like to offer you the role. To secure onboarding, pay a refundable £95 registration and background-check fee.

The job may not exist. In other cases, the "work" is routing criminal money through an account in your own name. This guide shows the warning signs, how to verify an agency, and what to do if you have already paid or shared details.

Why these scams are convincing

Scammers copy real agency names, logos, job-board posts, recruiter language, and email signatures. They may impersonate a real recruiter or use a lookalike domain that is only one character away from the real agency's domain.

An employment business cannot charge a work-seeker a fee for work-finding services. In Great Britain, Regulation 26 permits an employment agency — not an employment business — to charge a work-finding fee for Schedule 3 occupations, subject to detailed conditions; Northern Ireland has parallel separate rules. Those occupations are specified performers and creative occupations, photographic or fashion models, and professional sports people. Other narrow provisions exist, including certain publication-only services, and separate rules can apply to incorporated work-seekers. Optional non-work-finding services may be charged for, but access to work-finding cannot be made conditional on buying them.

A registration, release or admin fee tied to receiving a vacancy is therefore a serious warning and may breach the rules - but a prohibited or conditional charge does not prove that the company is fictitious. Treat it as the point to stop and verify the agency through routes you found yourself, not as the end of the enquiry.

Signs a recruitment agency is a scam

  • It asks you to pay upfront to secure the role, register, unlock onboarding, or release a job offer.
  • It says a check, certificate, equipment fee, or training fee must be paid to a personal or mismatched account.
  • It moves you off the job board to WhatsApp, Telegram, or a personal email almost immediately.
  • It asks for bank details, passport images, or ID documents with no explanation, through an unverified account or an insecure channel.
  • The pay is high for little work, or you are hired with no real interview.
  • A supposed job asks you to receive, hold, convert or forward client money through your personal bank account, payment account or crypto wallet.
  • The agency's name, domain, email, Companies House record, and website do not line up. A related version recruits you as a paid 'mystery shopper' and pays with a cheque that later bounces — see our mystery shopper scam guide.

How the scam works

First, a recruiter contacts you or replies to an application with a strong offer. Second, they move you off-platform and offer the role quickly. Third, they ask for a fee, identity documents, bank details, or a payment-processing task. Fourth, you pay, hand over documents, or let money pass through an account in your own name. Finally, the job disappears, the fee is gone, your identity is misused, or your account is frozen because it was used to move criminal money.

The most effective protection is to verify the agency before paying or sharing anything sensitive.

How to check an agency is genuine

Check the agency itself, not the role it is dangling in front of you.

Do not pay merely to secure or unlock a job. A genuine criminal-record check is a separate service that can carry a published fee. DBS covers work in England and Wales, Disclosure Scotland covers work in Scotland, and AccessNI covers work in Northern Ireland. Which criminal-record service applies depends on the role and where it is based. Individuals can apply directly for a basic DBS check, a Level 1 disclosure or a basic AccessNI check. Higher-level checks are restricted to eligible roles and normally involve an employer, organisation or registered body.

Level 2 applications are organisation-started; most PVG applications are also organisation-started, with separate routes for personal assistants, self-employed people and people working for an individual. Verify the role, level, route and current fee on the relevant government service. Never pay a private account or a rushed recruiter link.

  • A fee to register, to be put forward, or to release an offer is a serious warning, because an agency generally cannot charge an individual work-seeker for finding work — and a separately offered service can only be charged for where access to work-finding is not made conditional on buying it.
  • Find the agency independently through its official website and a phone number you find yourself.
  • If it claims to be a UK limited company, compare the name, company number, address, and directors on Companies House. Companies House shows the registry record and current recorded status; it does not prove that the business, vacancy or person contacting you is genuine, and filed information is not necessarily verified.
  • Check that the recruiter's email is on the real agency domain, not a free or lookalike address.
  • Ring the switchboard number on the agency's own site and ask whether the consultant who contacted you works there.
  • Expect some document checks early: an employment business may be required to confirm your identity before introducing you to a hirer, which can include sending you for interview or submitting your CV. Ask why each item is needed and use the confirmed secure process - the unsafe feature is an unexplained request through an unverified contact, not the timing.
  • Walk away from any role that asks you to receive, hold, convert or forward a client's money through your own personal bank account, payment account or crypto wallet.

If you are unsure whether a recruiter's site is genuine, our guide on checking whether a website is a scam helps, and our Indeed job scam guide covers the same trick on job boards.

If you paid or shared details

Tell your bank or card issuer the same day, using the number printed on your card, that the payment was obtained by fraud. Identity documents and financial information could be reused for identity fraud. Secure affected accounts and check the files held by Experian, Equifax and TransUnion. Consider Cifas Protective Registration, £30 for two years, only where the exposure puts your identity at heightened risk; check Cifas's current criteria. Our scam recovery checklist sets out the sequence.

How to report a recruitment-agency scam (UK)

There are two separate reports worth making, and the second one depends on where the agency is based.

The first is the crime: Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or on 0300 123 2040 covers England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and Police Scotland on 101 covers Scotland. It also has a route for reporting something suspicious where nobody responded and no money was lost.

The second is the regulatory report. For agency conduct in England, Scotland or Wales, use the Fair Work Agency. If the employment business or agency is based in Northern Ireland, the Employment Agency Inspectorate is likely to be its regulator. The Fair Work Agency began operating on 7 April 2026 and replaced the Employment Agency Standards Inspectorate; its complaint route is published on GOV.UK as "Making a complaint to the Fair Work Agency about your recruitment agency", and the Employment Agency Inspectorate's details are on economy-ni.gov.uk.

Either can look at an agency charging work-seekers even where you lost no money yourself.

Also tell the job board the listing appeared on. For an SMS, forward the message to 7726. For WhatsApp, Telegram or Signal, preserve the evidence and use the app's report and block tools; 7726 is not the in-app reporting route. The NCSC takes phishing emails at report@phishing.gov.uk. Our scam recovery checklist covers securing accounts and preserving evidence.

Frequently asked questions

Can a UK recruitment agency charge me a fee to find work?

Generally not for finding work. Charging an individual work-seeker for finding or trying to find work is prohibited, with separate regulations in Great Britain and Northern Ireland and defined Schedule 3 exceptions for specified performing, creative, modelling and professional-sport occupations. An optional service unrelated to work-finding may be charged for, provided access to work-finding is not conditional on buying it. So a fee to register, to be put forward, or to release an offer is a serious warning and may breach the rules — stop and verify the agency independently before paying anything or sending documents. A prohibited charge is not, by itself, proof that the company does not exist.

A recruiter wants my bank details and passport before an interview - red flag?

A request through an unverified WhatsApp account or lookalike email is a serious warning. However, a verified employment business may need to check identity and right-to-work evidence before introducing you to a hirer. Verify the agency through contact details found independently, ask why the documents are required, and use its confirmed secure process. Supply bank details only when the verified agency or employer genuinely needs them for payroll.

The agency asked me to receive and forward money - is that a job?

No. Being asked to receive, hold, convert or forward a client's money through your personal bank account, payment account or crypto wallet is a money-mule red flag, whatever the job title says. Genuine finance roles do not run client money through an employee's own accounts. Stop immediately, do not move any more money, and tell your bank.

I have already paid a recruiter - can I get my money back?

Possibly. If you paid by card, ask your bank about disputing the payment. If you sent a bank transfer, the APP reimbursement rules may apply to an eligible domestic consumer transfer sent over Faster Payments or retail CHAPS on or after 7 October 2024. Reimbursement is capped at £85,000, has to be claimed within 13 months and is subject to exclusions, and a firm may deduct an excess of no more than £100 - which it cannot apply to a consumer it assesses as vulnerable. None of it is a guaranteed refund.

How do I report a recruitment-agency scam?

Make two reports. Report Fraud, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland, takes the fraud itself. For agency conduct in England, Scotland or Wales, use the Fair Work Agency; if the employment business or agency is based in Northern Ireland, the Employment Agency Inspectorate is likely to be its regulator. Tell the job board as well, and your bank the same day if money moved through your account.
